listenings.text: I have been a guide inside this cathedral for eleven years, and I always start in the same place: with your back to the door, looking up. If you stand here at ten in the morning, the light comes through the small window on the left and lands on the mosaic above the altar. If you come at four, it lands on the floor instead, and nobody looks up at all. That is the whole secret of the building. The columns are Roman, taken from an older temple, and if you look closely at the third one you can still see the marks of the sea on the stone. Everything in here is ornate except the ceiling, which is completely plain, and that is not an accident. When the eye has nowhere else to go, it goes up.

People ask me for the best photograph in the old town, and my answer disappoints everybody. There is no good photograph of this street. If you stand at the end of it, the facades look flat and grey, because the phone cannot see the texture of the stone. If you stand under the archway instead and just wait, something else happens. The shade is cold, the noise changes, and you start hearing the water. So my advice is not about a camera. Walk the street once with the phone in your pocket, and describe it out loud to somebody who is not there. If you can make them see it, you have understood the place. Then take the photograph, if you still want one.

extra_audio.text: First he walked into the square from the narrow street on the north side, at ten in the morning. Then he stopped under the archway, because the shade there was cold and the noise of the street disappeared. After that he looked up at the facade and noticed that the stone was weathered on one side only, where the wind comes from the sea. At that point he saw the mosaic above the door, small and ornate, that nobody photographs because it is too high. In the end he put the phone in his pocket, sat down on the step, and stayed for an hour without taking a single picture.
